idea: Filter out documents that do not start with '= ... =' or contain WikiText-style tokens (' @-@ ', ' , ', ' . '), and shuffle the remaining clean documents with CURATE_SEED.
why: This immediately removes the bulk of irrelevant spam and non-WikiText noise while preserving all target-domain examples if the pool is sufficient to reach T tokens without padding.
outcome: dev 1.9071 against 1.9409 for the best at the time, KEPT as the new best

idea: Implement the exact deduplication step (lowercase + whitespace normalization hash) and the 'word-shuffled article' detection filter using the target_sample bigram set to drop pool docs that look like WikiText but have jumbled sentences, then shuffle and expand to T tokens.
why: Previous filters still allowed identical docs to repeat and allowed shuffled-word WikiText articles to contaminate the training distribution, reducing signal quality and hurting bpb.
outcome: dev 1.9335 against 1.9071 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Fit a LogisticRegression classifier using char n-grams on the first 2000 characters of docs (target_sample as positives, random pool sample as negatives) to score all pool documents, keep only high-scoring clean WikiText docs, deduplicate them exactly (hash of normalized first 200 chars), expand to T tokens if under the 0.35T threshold by appending lower-scoring clean docs, and shuffle the final order.
why: Combines strong structural domain filtering with a learned probabilistic score to aggressively prune spam/shuffled junk while preserving scarce clean WikiText context, and explicitly fills the shortage to ensure the trainer completes T steps rather than cycling high-noise undersampled text.
outcome: dev 1.9468 against 1.9071 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Use a 'first-line pattern match' filter to keep only documents starting with '= Language short title =' or '= IN国家标准/INNational ID Number =' for the specific target sample domains found in the target_sample, while excluding all non-matchers, then exactly deduplicate, shuffle, and ensure length.
why: The target_sample explicitly shows documents starting with a specific pattern '= Language title =' or similar IN-standard headers, and filtering by this strict header format significantly reduces noise from the non-target domains present in the current 1.9071 baseline.
outcome: dev 3.5446 against 1.9071 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Implement exact deduplication (normalize whitespace, hash first 200 chars) and remove word-shuffled documents using a target-driven bigram hit-rate threshold before shuffling and expanding to T tokens.
why: This combines the structural filtering of the random-order winner with the specific word-scramble detection and deduplication steps that were previously rejected only because they lacked an initial valid base, likely yielding higher purity without computational overload.
outcome: dev 1.9451 against 1.9071 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Implement strict domain filtering to keep only documents starting with '= ... =' AND containing at least one WikiText marker (like '@-@'), exact deduplication via hashing, and removal of documents with compressed size ratio < 0.2 (junk), then shuffle and expand to T tokens.
why: This directly replicates the highly successful combined filtering strategy (pattern match + WikiText markers) from run #1 but adds two specific optimizations (near-exact dedup and zlib compression check) that were mentioned in the winning run's notes to aggressively purge noisy data without inflating the token count with garbage.
outcome: dev 1.9322 against 1.9071 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: After filtering for WikiText headers and markers, apply exact and near-exact deduplication to remove exact and near-duplicate documents before shuffling the remaining clean documents to boost in-domain data quality.
why: This directly addresses the junk/duplicate removal rule from Exp 1 and mirrors the successful strategies in Exp 5 and Exp 6 while avoiding the heavy shuffling-heavy bigram filters that increased BPs in Exp 2 and Exp 5.
outcome: dev 1.9326 against 1.9071 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Fit a LogisticRegression classifier on the first 500 characters of a seeded random sample of pool docs (positives = target_sample chunks, negatives = high-confidence WikiText docs) combined with structural features ('=...=' header and '@-@' markers) to score all docs, then filter to top 20%, apply strict Size>200/UniqueLines>0.5/Zlib>0.2/ASCII_ratio>0.8/Dedup rules, and expand the top-scoring filtered list to T tokens via the same seeded shuffle.
why: This combines weak supervision with robust structural/junk filters to systematically identify and prioritize high-quality in-domain text while explicitly avoiding the lossy or imbalanced approaches that degraded previous experiments.
outcome: dev 2.3322 against 1.9071 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Replace the simple string-based WikiText marker detection with a pre-trained Unigram+Bigram Word遮挡 model as implemented in the lead-setting dev bpb 1.8310 experiment to robustly reject mixed-domain articles and word-scrambled WikiText while keeping the clean header-filtered set.
why: The current marker-based filter likely mistakes mixed-domain mini-docs or word-scrambled articles as in-domain simply because they share the '= ... =' format or contain rare whitespace tokens, whereas a word-level bigram model trained on the target domain would effectively distinguish clean WikiText from scrambled or cross-domain text, directly addressing the ~$0.025 improvement seen in similar settings.
outcome: dev 1.9274 against 1.9071 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Filter only documents whose first 400 characters contain at least one of the specific WikiText tokenization characters ('@-@', '@,@', '@.@', ', ', ' . ') AND start with '= ... =', perform exact deduplication on the first 200 normalized chars, then shuffle and expand to T tokens.
why: The previous best header/marker filter (1.9071) failed to fully exclude word-scrambled WikiText articles (leading to 1.93+); increasing marker specificity and enforcing exact deduplication will reduce corruption while preserving clean positive samples, mirroring the successful 1.8225 baseline component.
outcome: dev 1.9341 against 1.9071 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: After the strict WikiText header and marker filtering and exact deduplication performed in the previous best run (1.9071), add a secondary filter to drop any remaining documents that have an unusually high compression ratio (zlib ratio > 0.8) or contain long stretches of repeated boilerplate lines (unique-line ratio < 0.3), before shuffling and expanding to T tokens.
why: This follows the successful pattern of the second-best run (1.8225) which used a simple junk ratio filter on cleaned data that was otherwise unoptimized, but applies it only to the clean subset to avoid the performance penalty of model training.
outcome: dev 1.9334 against 1.9071 for the best at the time, rejected

idea: Instead of requiring the '= ... =' header, retain documents that trigger the WikiText unigram/bigram filter but drop those with a low first-line similarity to any known WikiText sentence fragment (computed via cosine similarity between target_sample character n-grams and the doc's first 300 chars), combined with exact deduplication and expansion to T tokens.
why: The previous best run likely suffered from non-WikiText documents (like sci-fi fiction or math snippets) passing the simple marker head check; identifying the specific missing header pattern in the target set is impossible without network, so we must relax the structural requirement and rely on the 1.8300 transferable bigram-based domain detection to distinguish WikiText style from other non-junk, non-target domains.
outcome: dev 1.9269 against 1.9071 for the best at the time, rejected
